::: {.solutions}

Marks: **(M1)** method, **(A1)** accuracy, **(B1)** independent. Total **32**.

::: {.callout-important}
## What to watch while marking

1. **Did they answer the right question?** "Across the surface" and "through" both give clean surds. An
   answer of the wrong kind is $0$, however well presented.
2. **Did they compare unfoldings?** Q2(b), Q3 and Q4(c) each have a wrong route that produces a
   respectable-looking number. One unfolding with no comparison is not a complete answer.
3. **Q4(c) is the discriminating one.** The base is a face, so the base diagonal is a legal surface path —
   and it beats the lateral route. Most students never consider it.
:::

---

# Section A — Recall

## Question 1 **[4]**

::: {.question}
(a) Cube edge $a$: shortest path across the surface \_\_\_ and through \_\_\_; (b) height of a regular
tetrahedron of edge $a$; (c) cross-section at height $h$ is the base scaled by \_\_\_; (d)
$R_{\text{circum}}:r_{\text{in}}$ for a regular tetrahedron, and the volume ratio.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**(a) $a\sqrt5$ across; $a\sqrt3$ through. (B1)** *Both halves needed.* The first unfolds two faces into a
$2a\times a$ rectangle; the second is $\sqrt{a^{2}+a^{2}+a^{2}}$.

**(b) $\dfrac{a\sqrt6}{3}$, i.e. $a\sqrt{\tfrac23}$. (B1)** *From $H^{2}=a^{2}-\left(\tfrac{a}{\sqrt3}\right)^{2}$ —
the base circumradius of an equilateral triangle is $\tfrac{a}{\sqrt3}$.*

**(c) $1-\dfrac hH$. (B1)** *Accept $\dfrac{H-h}{H}$. **Do not** accept $\dfrac hH$, which is the standard
slip.*

**(d) $3:1$, so the volumes are $27:1$. (B1)** *Both halves needed.*
:::

---

## Question 2 **[4]**

::: {.question}
A cuboid has edges $2,3,6$. (a) the space diagonal; (b) the shortest surface path between opposite corners,
comparing all three unfoldings.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**(a) $7$. (B1)** &nbsp; $\sqrt{2^{2}+3^{2}+6^{2}}=\sqrt{4+9+36}=\sqrt{49}=7$.

**(b) $\sqrt{61}$. (M1 A1 A1)**

Unfolding two faces pairs **one** edge against the **sum of the other two**, and there are three pairings:

| pairing | rectangle | length |
|---|---|---|
| $6$ with $2+3=5$ | $6\times5$ | $\sqrt{36+25}=\sqrt{61}\approx7.81$ |
| $3$ with $2+6=8$ | $3\times8$ | $\sqrt{9+64}=\sqrt{73}\approx8.54$ |
| $2$ with $3+6=9$ | $2\times9$ | $\sqrt{4+81}=\sqrt{85}\approx9.22$ |

**M1** for producing a rectangle of the form (edge) $\times$ (sum of the other two); **A1** for $\sqrt{61}$;
**A1** for showing all three and selecting the smallest.

*The winner always pairs the **longest** edge with the sum of the two shortest — squaring punishes a large
sum more than a large single edge.*

**Marking.** One correct unfolding with no comparison: **M1 A1 only**, maximum $3$.
:::

---

# Section B — Standard

## Question 3 **[4]**

::: {.question}
Regular tetrahedron $OABC$ of edge $6$; $X$ is the midpoint of $OA$; $Y$ on $BC$ with $BY=2$. Shortest
surface distance $XY$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**$\sqrt{31}$. (M1 M1 A1 A1)**

**Unfold faces $OAB$ and $ABC$ about $AB$. (M1)** Both are equilateral of side $6$, so the net is a rhombus
and the path becomes the straight segment $XY$.

**Set up the triangle. (M1)** Let $Z$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Then

$$XZ=6 \ \ (\text{parallel and equal to } AC),\qquad ZY=BZ-BY=3-2=1,\qquad \angle XZY=60^{\circ}.$$

**Cosine rule. (A1)**

$$XY^{2}=6^{2}+1^{2}-2(6)(1)\cos60^{\circ}=36+1-6=31 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad XY=\sqrt{31}\approx5.57 .$$

**Compare the alternatives. (A1)** Unfolding about $OB$ gives the same $31$ by symmetry; going round
through face $OAC$ is longer. So $\sqrt{31}$ is the shortest.

*This is the archive's anchor question ([JZ Mock A P2 Q15](../../mocks/jz_mock_a/paper2_ms.qmd)) with
the numbers changed — there, edge $12$ and $BY=3$ give $3\sqrt{13}$.*
:::

---

## Question 4 **[4]**

::: {.question}
Square-based pyramid $ABCDT$, all edges $4$. (a) height; (b) apex to the midpoint of a base edge;
(c) shortest surface path from $A$ to $C$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**(a) $2\sqrt2$. (B1)** The base circumradius is half the diagonal, $\dfrac{4\sqrt2}{2}=2\sqrt2$, so

$$H^{2}=4^{2}-\left(2\sqrt2\right)^{2}=16-8=8 ,\qquad H=2\sqrt2 .$$

**(b) $2\sqrt3$. (B1)** Every lateral face is **equilateral** of side $4$ (all edges equal), and this
distance is that triangle's altitude: $\dfrac{4\sqrt3}{2}=2\sqrt3$.

**(c) $4\sqrt2$ — straight across the base. (M1 A1)**

**M1** for considering **both** kinds of route:

| route | length |
|---|---|
| across the **base**, along diagonal $AC$ | $4\sqrt2\approx5.66$ |
| over the two lateral faces $ABT$ and $BCT$ | $4\sqrt3\approx6.93$ |

*(For the lateral route, unfold about $BT$: with $B=(0,0)$, $T=(4,0)$, the two base vertices land at
$(2,\pm2\sqrt3)$, giving $AC=4\sqrt3$.)*

**A1** for $4\sqrt2$.

**Marking — this is the question that separates.** The base **is** one of the five faces, so the base
diagonal is a legitimate surface path, and it wins. A candidate who answers $4\sqrt3$ has done the harder
piece of work correctly and still lost the mark, because they assumed "along the surface" meant "over the
sloping faces". Award **M1** for a correct lateral unfolding, **0** for the accuracy mark.
:::

---

## Question 5 **[4]**

::: {.question}
Cube of edge $1$. A face has diagonal $d$. Find the perpendicular distance from a vertex directly above one
end of $d$ to the line $d$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**$1$. (M1 A1 A1 B1)**

Put the cube as $[0,1]^{3}$, let $d$ run from $(0,0,0)$ to $(1,1,0)$ on the base, and take the vertex
$P=(0,0,1)$, directly above $(0,0,0)$.

**Method 4 — area over base. (M1 A1)**

$$\text{area of the triangle}=\tfrac12\left\lvert(0,0,1)\times(1,1,0)\right\rvert
=\tfrac12\left\lvert(-1,1,0)\right\rvert=\frac{\sqrt2}{2},
\qquad d(P,\ell)=\frac{2\times\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}{\sqrt2}=1 .$$

**Or the three perpendiculars theorem. (M1 A1)** $P$ is directly above $H=(0,0,0)$, which **lies on** the
line, so the perpendicular from $H$ to the line has length $0$ and

$$d=\sqrt{PH^{2}+0^{2}}=PH=1 .$$

**A1** for the exact value $1$. **B1** for naming the method.

*The answer is the edge length, and the reason is the special position: because $P$ sits directly above a
point **of** the line, the perpendicular is just the vertical edge. Spotting that is worth more than the
computation — a candidate who reaches $1$ by cross product has the mark, but one who sees why has the
minute.*
:::

## Question 6 **[4]**

::: {.question}
Cone height $H$, base radius $R$; inscribed cylinder. (a) radius at height $h$; (b) the maximising height;
(c) the volume ratio.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**(a) (B1)** The cone above height $h$ is **similar** to the whole cone, with height $H-h$, so every length
scales by $\dfrac{H-h}{H}=1-\dfrac hH$. The cross-sectional radius is therefore
$R\left(1-\dfrac hH\right)$. ∎

**(b) $h=\dfrac H3$. (M1 A1)**

$$V=\pi R^{2}\left(1-\frac hH\right)^{2}h .$$

Differentiating (or maximising $h\left(1-\tfrac hH\right)^{2}$):

$$\frac{dV}{dh}=\pi R^{2}\left[\left(1-\frac hH\right)^{2}-\frac{2h}{H}\left(1-\frac hH\right)\right]
=\pi R^{2}\left(1-\frac hH\right)\left(1-\frac{3h}{H}\right)=0 ,$$

so $h=H$ (giving zero volume) or $h=\dfrac H3$. **The maximum is $h=\dfrac H3$.**

**(c) $\dfrac49$. (A1)** At $h=\tfrac H3$ the radius is $\tfrac{2R}{3}$, so

$$V_{\text{cyl}}=\pi\left(\frac{2R}{3}\right)^{2}\cdot\frac H3=\frac{4\pi R^{2}H}{27},
\qquad
\frac{V_{\text{cyl}}}{V_{\text{cone}}}=\frac{4\pi R^{2}H/27}{\pi R^{2}H/3}=\frac49 .$$

*Compare the pyramid version on the clinic page, where the answer is $\tfrac{\pi}{9}$ — the method is
identical and only the base shape changes.*
:::

# Section C — Stretch

## Question 7 **[4]**

::: {.question}
Sphere inscribed in a cube of edge $a$, cube inscribed in a larger sphere. (a) the two radii; (b) the ratio
of the volumes in the form $k\sqrt3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**(a) (B1 B1)**

- **Inscribed sphere:** it touches each face, so its diameter is the edge: $r=\dfrac a2$.
- **Circumscribed sphere:** it passes through every vertex, so its diameter is the **space diagonal**
  $a\sqrt3$: $R=\dfrac{a\sqrt3}{2}$.

*The two are the two natural "radii" of a cube, and the distinction — face versus vertex — is the whole of
part (a).*

**(b) $3\sqrt3$. (M1 A1)**

$$\frac Rr=\frac{a\sqrt3/2}{a/2}=\sqrt3
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\frac{V_{\text{outer}}}{V_{\text{inner}}}=\left(\sqrt3\right)^{3}=3\sqrt3 \approx5.196 .$$

**M1** for cubing the length ratio; **A1** for $3\sqrt3$.

*Common error: giving $\sqrt3$ or $3$ — the volume ratio is the **cube** of the length ratio, and
$\left(\sqrt3\right)^{3}$ is $3\sqrt3$, not $3$.*
:::

## Question 8 **[4]**

::: {.question}
Regular tetrahedron $OABC$ of edge $a$. (a) prove $OA\perp BC$ using the cube embedding; (b) find the
distance between the midpoints of $OA$ and $BC$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**(a) (M1 A1)**

**Place the vertices at alternate corners of a cube of edge $2$: (M1)**

$$O=(1,1,1),\quad A=(1,-1,-1),\quad B=(-1,1,-1),\quad C=(-1,-1,1).$$

Each pair is $2\sqrt2$ apart — for instance $O-A=(0,2,2)$ has length $2\sqrt2$ — so this really is a
regular tetrahedron, of edge $a=2\sqrt2$.

**Then (A1)**

$$\overrightarrow{OA}=(0,-2,-2),\qquad \overrightarrow{BC}=(0,-2,2),\qquad
\overrightarrow{OA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=0+4-4=0 ,$$

so $OA\perp BC$. ∎ *By symmetry the same holds for all three pairs of opposite edges.*

**(b) $\dfrac{a}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{a\sqrt2}{2}$. (M1 A1)**

The midpoints are

$$M=\tfrac12(O+A)=(1,0,0),\qquad N=\tfrac12(B+C)=(-1,0,0),$$

so $MN=2$. Scaling from the edge $2\sqrt2$ to a general edge $a$:

$$\frac{MN}{a}=\frac{2}{2\sqrt2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad MN=\frac{a}{\sqrt2}.$$

**Check at $a=2\sqrt2$:** $\dfrac{2\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}=2$ ✓

*Accept any correct method for (b), including dropping a perpendicular and using $MN^{2}=
\left(\tfrac{a\sqrt3}{2}\right)^{2}-\left(\tfrac a2\right)^{2}$ — the median of a face minus half an edge.
But the cube embedding makes both parts fall out at once, which is why it is worth memorising.*
:::

---

::: {.callout-tip}
## The thread through this paper

**Q2(b), Q3 and Q4(c) are the same instruction three times: enumerate the routes.** Each has a plausible
wrong answer available — $\sqrt{73}$, the long way round the tetrahedron, and $4\sqrt3$ — and each is
reached by a candidate who did correct mathematics on the first route that occurred to them.

That is the habit the clinic exists to build: [unfolding is cheap, and guessing the route is not]{.hl}.
:::

:::
